title: Groaning creation (Romans 8:18–27)
hookLine: the whole creation groans in labor; the Spirit prays in groans too deep for words
last: A CHILD AT HOME, NOT A PRISONER ON TRIAL.

lines: A HOSPITAL ROOM, NOTHING TO SAY.
A BREATH THAT ISN'T QUITE A WORD.
cards: A hospital room, late. Someone sits beside the bed with nothing left to say. Outside, after the bad news, all that comes out is a long breath, not quite a word.

Prayer is often pictured as sentences, nicely put, in the right order. Then comes a moment when the sentences are gone. In the middle of Romans chapter eight, Paul stops to talk about exactly that, and he widens it.
It isn't only one person who groans, he says. It's the whole world. And then he says something about God and the prayers that have no words.

teach.b: Paul starts honestly: there is suffering now. "For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us."
He doesn't deny the suffering; he sets it beside something bigger. Then he turns to the whole created world, oceans, forests, animals, and says it's waiting too.
The King James calls it the earnest expectation of the creature: like someone on tiptoe at a window. "For we know that the whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now."
Travaileth means the pains of labor. So the groaning isn't a death rattle; it's a birth. Something new is coming, and the world is in labor with it.

Then he brings it home: "Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered."
Three groans, then. Creation groans. We groan.
And, Paul says, the Spirit of God groans with us, underneath our words, when we have none. That we includes Paul.
For him, the prayer doesn't depend on getting the words right. Some Christians say this verse gives them permission to pray with tears, or a sigh, or silence.
Some Pentecostal and charismatic Christians connect it with praying in tongues; others read it as the silent prayer of the heart. Both readings find the same promise: nobody groans alone.

how: Some Christians lean on Romans 8:26 when they cannot find words, praying in silence, with tears or with a sigh; some Pentecostal and charismatic Christians also connect it with praying in tongues.

a world crying out in its final death pains

games.q: what's inside the groaning — tap the pairs.

s: Paul says prayer only counts if the words are right
"we know not what we should pray for as we ought", and the Spirit prays with groanings which cannot be uttered.
Paul pictures creation's groaning as labor pains
travaileth: the world in labor with something new.
Paul says present suffering isn't real
he names it, then says it is not worthy to be compared with the glory to come.

games.q: you're sitting with someone in grief and have no words to pray. what does Paul say happens?
o: the prayer doesn't count until you find words.
the Spirit prays with groans too deep for words.
you should wait until you feel better.
games.why: "the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered." nobody groans alone.

practice: Bring to mind something too big or too tangled for sentences: a person who's sick, the state of the world, something in you that you can't name. Don't explain it; just breathe in and let out one long, slow sigh, then another.
If you pray, let the sigh be the prayer, and remember Paul says the Spirit is praying with it; if you don't, let the sighs carry what words can't.
